question: Which laboratory pattern best supports severe iron depletion?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Severe iron depletion decreases ferritin, while variable red-cell size increases RDW.
The ferritin change fits, but RDW is expected to increase. A decreased RDW would require uniform red-cell size.
The RDW change fits, but severe iron depletion lowers ferritin. Increased ferritin would require preserved or increased iron stores.
Both changes oppose the described iron-deficiency pattern. This would require a disorder with increased iron storage and reduced binding capacity.
Severe depletion should lower ferritin, and TIBC is normal or increased. This pattern would require preserved stores with reduced binding capacity.

question: Which protein normally limits platelet-rich microvascular thrombosis by cleaving endothelial von Willebrand factor?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Activated protein C inactivates Factors Va and VIIIa rather than cleaving endothelial vWF. It would be correct if the task concerned regulation of Factor V activity.
ADAMTS13 cleaves vWF and thereby limits accumulation of platelet-vWF thrombi in the microvasculature.
Factor VIII participates in coagulation and is stabilized by vWF. It would be correct if the task asked which factor has a shortened half-life with dysfunctional vWF.
Factor XI deficiency causes hemophilia C and does not explain vWF cleavage. It would be correct if the task asked which factor is deficient in hemophilia C.
Factor IX deficiency causes hemophilia B and does not cleave vWF. It would be correct if the task asked which factor is deficient in hemophilia B.

question: Which inheritance pattern characterizes hemophilia C?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Hemophilia C is not described as X-linked dominant. This choice would require transmission through an X-linked dominant trait.
Autosomal dominant inheritance is associated with many cases of von Willebrand disease, not hemophilia C. That diagnosis would make this pattern appropriate.
Hemophilia C results from Factor XI deficiency and follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
X-linked recessive inheritance characterizes hemophilia A and B. Either Factor VIII or Factor IX deficiency would make this correct.
Hemophilia C is not maternally inherited through mitochondria. This would require a mitochondrial disorder rather than Factor XI deficiency.

question: Which diagnostic procedure establishes Hodgkin lymphoma when an involved node is accessible?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: A peripheral smear is part of the initial blood-disorder evaluation but does not establish Hodgkin lymphoma. It would be appropriate for evaluating circulating cellular abnormalities.
Serum protein electrophoresis may be considered when malignancy is suspected but does not identify diagnostic nodal histology. It would be appropriate when evaluating abnormal serum proteins.
Bone marrow transplantation is a management option rather than the establishing diagnostic procedure. It would fit a treatment question after diagnosis.
Excisional biopsy permits identification of Reed-Sternberg cells and establishes the diagnosis before staging.
The ristocetin assay evaluates platelet aggregation in von Willebrand disease. It would be correct for suspected mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal vWF function.

question: A blood sample continues generating thrombin after activated protein C is added. Which abnormality best explains this result?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Reduced Factor VIII produces bleeding rather than resistance to activated protein C. It would fit hemophilia A or some forms of von Willebrand disease.
Reduced Factor IX produces hemophilia B rather than persistent thrombin formation. It would be correct with an X-linked bleeding disorder.
Reduced Factor XI causes hemophilia C and does not cause activated protein C resistance. It would fit autosomal recessive mucocutaneous bleeding.
Reduced ADAMTS13 causes platelet-vWF microthrombi rather than this clotting-test result. Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia would make it appropriate.
Factor V Leiden causes Factor Va to resist activated protein C, permitting continued thrombin production.

question: A patient has microcytosis, increased RDW, and markedly reduced iron stores after gastric bypass. Which paired abnormality is most consistent?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin and produces a normal or increased TIBC, particularly with severe depletion.
The hemoglobin change fits, but iron deficiency does not characteristically lower TIBC. Reduced binding capacity would require a different laboratory pattern.
The TIBC may rise, but anemia requires reduced hemoglobin. High hemoglobin would require increased rather than reduced red-cell mass.
Low ferritin fits depleted stores, but high hemoglobin conflicts with anemia. Preserved or increased red-cell mass would be needed.
Both findings conflict with the described anemia and anisocytosis. This would require preserved red-cell mass with uniform cell size.

question: An older adult with chronic poor nutrition has macrocytosis, cognitive decline, and absent vibration sensation in both feet. Which deficiency best unifies these findings?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A, not macrocytic anemia with neurologic findings. Joint or muscle bleeding with prolonged PTT would make it appropriate.
Vitamin B12 deficiency links macrocytic anemia with dementia and peripheral neuropathy affecting vibratory sensation.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia. Schistocytes and a markedly reduced platelet count would support it.
Factor XI deficiency causes hemophilia C rather than macrocytosis and neuropathy. Trauma-associated mucocutaneous bleeding would make it appropriate.
Reduced vWF causes a bleeding disorder, not this neurologic-macrocytic syndrome. Epistaxis, bruising, or procedure-related bleeding would support it.

question: A hemoglobin point mutation replaces one β-chain amino acid and promotes red-cell deformation during infection. Which molecular change is responsible?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: This reverses the stated sickle mutation. It would be correct only if the direction of amino-acid substitution were reversed.
The source identifies valine, not glycine, as the replacement. Glycine would require a different point mutation.
This describes the relevant substitution, but the option does not identify the downstream molecular event asked by the stem. It would be correct if the lead-in asked for the amino-acid replacement.
The glutamic-acid-to-valine substitution permits hemoglobin S polymerization during infection, hypoxia, acidosis, or high altitude.
Stress promotes polymerization rather than cleavage of hemoglobin S. Cleavage would require a proteolytic mechanism not described here.

question: A patient has schistocytes, profound thrombocytopenia, and normal PT and PTT. Which intravascular material is accumulating?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: The described process centers on platelet-vWF thrombi, not Factor IX. Factor IX deficiency would instead support hemophilia B.
Factor VIII is stabilized by vWF but is not the named principal component of these microthrombi. This pairing would require a Factor VIII-centered process.
Activated protein C regulates Factors Va and VIIIa rather than forming the microthrombi. Its relevance would increase in a Factor V Leiden evaluation.
ADAMTS13 normally limits thrombosis and is deficient or inhibited, so it does not accumulate in the thrombi. This would require preserved enzyme deposition.
Reduced ADAMTS13 activity allows platelet-vWF thrombi to accumulate throughout the microvasculature.

question: Which pairing correctly matches a bleeding disorder with its characteristic manifestation?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Hemophilia A causes deep bleeding, especially hemarthroses and large-muscle hemorrhage.
Hemophilia B more characteristically causes joint and large-muscle bleeding. Isolated epistaxis would better support a mucosal bleeding disorder.
Hemophilia C is associated with mucocutaneous bleeding after trauma or procedures. Recurrent large-joint bleeding would favor hemophilia A or B.
Type 1 von Willebrand disease causes bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and procedure-related bleeding. Renal infarction would support a vaso-occlusive disorder.
Factor V Leiden causes venous thrombosis rather than dental bleeding. A coagulation-factor or vWF disorder would make bleeding after dentistry appropriate.

question: Why may alternate-day oral iron produce greater absorption than daily administration?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: The stated explanation involves hepcidin-mediated absorption, not suppressed ferritin production. This would require ferritin regulation to be the limiting mechanism.
Daily oral iron increases hepcidin, which decreases iron absorption for approximately the next 48 hours.
The direction is reversed; daily dosing increases hepcidin. Decreased hepcidin would be expected to improve rather than limit absorption.
Alternate-day dosing is intended to improve absorption, not increase blood loss. This would require an unrelated bleeding effect.
The benefit is not attributed to reduced TIBC. This would require iron-binding capacity to control short-term absorption.

question: A patient has dysfunctional von Willebrand factor and a shortened Factor VIII half-life. Which disease subtype best fits?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Type 1 includes decreased vWF protein level and function, whereas the stem emphasizes functional impairment. Reduced quantity plus function would make type 1 appropriate.
Type 3 involves production of no vWF and is the most severe form. Complete absence rather than functional reduction would make it correct.
Type 2 features decreased vWF function, impairing Factor VIII stabilization and shortening its half-life.
Hemophilia A directly reflects Factor VIII deficiency rather than dysfunctional vWF. Deep joint or muscle bleeding without a vWF defect would support it.
Hemophilia C is Factor XI deficiency and does not explain reduced vWF function. Low Factor XI levels would make it correct.

question: Which combination represents two components of Virchow triad?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: These are blood-count abnormalities rather than components of Virchow triad. They would fit a cytopenia-focused evaluation.
These may accompany acute chest syndrome but are not Virchow-triad components. A pulmonary sickle complication would make them relevant.
These findings occur in TTP/HUS but do not constitute Virchow triad. Schistocytes and thrombocytopenia would support that pairing.
Virchow triad consists of blood-flow stasis, vessel-wall injury, and hypercoagulability.
This pairing can suggest vitamin B12 deficiency but is unrelated to Virchow triad. Neuropathy and low B12 would make it relevant.

question: A patient with sickle cell anemia cannot tolerate hydroxyurea. Which alternative directly reduces cellular adhesion to activated endothelium?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Caplacizumab targets vWF in severe TTP rather than P-selectin in sickle disease. Severe platelet-vWF microthrombosis would make it appropriate.
Rituximab is included in TTP management and does not provide the specified anti-adhesion mechanism. Immune-mediated ADAMTS13 deficiency would make it appropriate.
Emicizumab mimics Factor VIII activity in hemophilia A. Factor VIII deficiency would make it appropriate.
Desmopressin releases stored vWF and is used in type 1 von Willebrand disease or active hemophilia A management. A bleeding disorder would make it appropriate.
Crizanlizumab binds P-selectin on activated endothelial cells, reducing sickle-cell adhesion and vaso-occlusive crises.

question: A patient with suspected malignancy has painless cervical nodes, night sweats, and splenomegaly. Which test provides definitive diagnostic tissue?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Excisional biopsy demonstrates nodal architecture and permits identification of Reed-Sternberg cells.
A CBC is part of initial evaluation but does not provide diagnostic tissue. It would be sufficient only for identifying blood-count abnormalities.
Calcium may be considered when malignancy is suspected but does not establish Hodgkin lymphoma. It would answer a metabolic-evaluation question.
LDH may support malignancy evaluation but is not tissue diagnosis. It would be useful for laboratory assessment rather than histologic confirmation.
A smear is an initial hematologic test but cannot establish Reed-Sternberg histology in a node. It would fit evaluation of circulating-cell morphology.

question: A 52-year-old woman with prior gastric bypass has progressive fatigue, pallor, and spoon-shaped nails. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL [12-16 g/dL], MCV is 62 fL [80-96 fL], and ferritin is 3.2 ng/mL [20-300 ng/mL]. Which management plan is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Vitamin B12 treats macrocytic deficiency, whereas this patient has severe microcytic iron depletion. Macrocytosis with low B12 would make it correct.
Severe iron-deficiency anemia requires oral or intravenous iron, possible transfusion depending on severity, and identification and treatment of the underlying cause.
Factor VIII replacement treats hemophilia A, not depleted iron stores. Deep bleeding with low Factor VIII would make it appropriate.
This regimen treats TTP, which requires thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolysis. Schistocytes with severe thrombocytopenia would make it appropriate.
This is chronic sickle-cell management and does not replenish iron. Recurrent vaso-occlusive crises with hemoglobin S would make it appropriate.

question: An 85-year-old woman with poor intake has confusion and reduced vibration sensation in both feet. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL [12-16 g/dL], MCV is 109 fL [80-96 fL], and serum B12 is 105 ng/mL [200-900 ng/mL]. Which treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Iron treats iron-deficiency microcytosis, not macrocytosis with neuropathy. Low ferritin and MCV would make it appropriate.
vWF concentrate treats von Willebrand disease, not nutritional macrocytic anemia. Procedure-related mucosal bleeding with deficient vWF would support it.
Vitamin B12 replacement addresses the macrocytic anemia and neurologic manifestations while the underlying nutritional cause is treated.
Factor IX concentrate treats hemophilia B. X-linked deep-tissue bleeding with low Factor IX would make it correct.
Fresh frozen plasma supplies Factor XI in hemophilia C. Trauma-related mucocutaneous bleeding with Factor XI deficiency would make it appropriate.

question: An 18-year-old man with sickle cell anemia develops severe limb pain after a respiratory infection. He is afebrile, his lungs are clear, and no infiltrate is reported. Which immediate treatment bundle is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: This combination treats TTP rather than a vaso-occlusive crisis. Schistocytes and profound thrombocytopenia would make it appropriate.
Desmopressin and Factor VIII treat active hemophilia A bleeding. A prolonged PTT with deep hemorrhage would support this choice.
These are chronic preventive or curative strategies, not the immediate bundle for an acute pain crisis. Long-term disease modification would make them relevant.
Acute vaso-occlusive crisis management includes oxygen, intravenous hydration, pain control, and evaluation and empiric treatment for infection.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome with hypoxia, while radiation is unrelated. A chest infiltrate and hypoxia would support exchange transfusion.

question: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell anemia develops chest pain after a pain crisis. Oxygen saturation is 84% [95-100%], leukocyte count is 17,000/mm3 [4,500-11,000/mm3], and chest radiography shows a new infiltrate. Which next treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Iron does not treat hypoxic acute chest syndrome. Microcytosis with low ferritin would make iron replacement appropriate.
Desmopressin supports hemostasis in hemophilia A or type 1 vWD. Active bleeding with one of those disorders would make it appropriate.
Rituximab is part of TTP treatment, not acute chest management. Microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia would make it appropriate.
Crizanlizumab prevents future vaso-occlusive crises but is not the indicated intervention for current hypoxic acute chest syndrome. Chronic prevention would make it relevant.
A new infiltrate, leukocytosis, chest pain, and hypoxia indicate acute chest syndrome, for which exchange transfusion is recommended.

question: A 38-year-old man develops bloody diarrhea followed by pallor and petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.1 g/dL [13.5-17.5 g/dL], platelets are 15,000/mm3 [150,000-450,000/mm3], creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL [0.6-1.3 mg/dL], and PT and PTT are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Bloody diarrhea followed by microangiopathic hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and kidney injury supports Shiga-toxin-associated HUS.
Hemophilia A causes Factor VIII deficiency with prolonged PTT and deep bleeding, not thrombocytopenic microangiopathy. An isolated prolonged PTT would support it.
Factor V Leiden causes venous thrombosis rather than schistocyte-producing hemolysis and thrombocytopenia. DVT or pulmonary embolism would support it.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia with neurologic manifestations, not an acute diarrheal microangiopathy. Macrocytosis and low B12 would support it.
Hodgkin lymphoma presents with painless nodes and constitutional symptoms rather than acute bloody diarrhea and thrombocytopenia. Reed-Sternberg cells would support it.

question: A patient has confusion, schistocytes, and a platelet count of 12,000/mm3 [150,000-450,000/mm3]. PT and PTT are normal, and severe ADAMTS13 deficiency is suspected. Which next management is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Factor IX concentrate treats hemophilia B, which produces deep bleeding and prolonged PTT. Low Factor IX activity would make it appropriate.
TTP is almost always fatal without treatment and requires therapeutic plasma exchange plus glucocorticoids and rituximab.
Vitamin B12 does not treat platelet-vWF microthrombi. Macrocytosis, neuropathy, and low B12 would make it appropriate.
This is chronic sickle-cell management rather than emergency TTP treatment. Recurrent sickle crises would make it appropriate.
This treats active hemophilia A bleeding and would not remove an ADAMTS13 inhibitor. Deep bleeding with low Factor VIII would make it appropriate.

question: A critically ill patient with platelet-vWF microthrombi remains severely affected despite plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and rituximab. Which additional agent directly targets the adhesive protein in these thrombi?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Crizanlizumab binds endothelial P-selectin to prevent sickle-cell adhesion. Recurrent vaso-occlusive crises would make it appropriate.
Emicizumab mimics Factor VIII activity in hemophilia A. Factor VIII deficiency requiring prophylaxis would support it.
Caplacizumab is an anti-vWF monoclonal antibody considered for severe TTP.
Rituximab is already part of the described regimen and does not directly target vWF. The question would be correct if asking for standard immune-directed therapy.
Hydroxyurea is preventive therapy for sickle cell anemia, not severe TTP. Chronic vaso-occlusive disease would make it appropriate.

question: An 18-year-old man develops a massive thigh hematoma after minor trauma. PTT is 98 seconds [25-35 seconds], PT is normal, and platelet count is 110,000/mm3 [150,000-450,000/mm3]. Which deficiency most likely explains the deep-tissue bleeding pattern?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: vWF disorders more often cause bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and procedure-related bleeding. A mucosal pattern would make this more appropriate.
The source discusses activated protein C in Factor V Leiden testing, not as the cause of this bleeding pattern. Thrombosis rather than hemorrhage would redirect evaluation.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombocytopenic microangiopathy with schistocytes. Those findings rather than isolated deep bleeding would make it appropriate.
Hemophilia A causes large-muscle and joint bleeding with normal PT and prolonged PTT.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia and neurologic findings rather than isolated coagulation failure. Macrocytosis and neuropathy would support it.

question: A patient with known hemophilia A presents with active large-muscle bleeding. Which acute treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma is the listed treatment for hemophilia C because it contains Factor XI. Factor XI deficiency would make it appropriate.
Factor IX concentrate treats hemophilia B. Documented Factor IX deficiency would make it correct.
vWF concentrate treats von Willebrand disease rather than direct Factor VIII deficiency. Deficient or dysfunctional vWF would support it.
This regimen treats TTP and does not replace Factor VIII. Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia would make it appropriate.
Active hemophilia A bleeding is treated with desmopressin plus Factor VIII replacement.

question: A 21-year-old man has persistent postoperative oozing. PTT is 82 seconds [25-35 seconds], PT is normal, Factor VIII activity is 42% [50-150%], and ristocetin produces no platelet aggregation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Procedure-related oozing, reduced Factor VIII, and absent ristocetin-induced aggregation indicate deficient or dysfunctional vWF.
Hemophilia B reflects Factor IX deficiency and does not explain abnormal ristocetin aggregation. Low Factor IX with deep bleeding would support it.

Hemophilia C reflects Factor XI deficiency and usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding after trauma or procedures, but it does not produce the stated ristocetin defect. Low Factor XI would make it correct.
Factor V Leiden produces thrombosis through activated protein C resistance rather than postoperative oozing. Venous thromboembolism would support it.
TTP causes thrombocytopenia and schistocytic hemolysis with normal coagulation studies. Those findings would make it appropriate.

question: A patient with type 1 von Willebrand disease has excessive bleeding after a dental procedure. Which treatment should be given first to mobilize endogenous hemostatic protein?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Factor IX concentrate treats hemophilia B. Factor IX deficiency would make it appropriate.
Desmopressin releases vWF stored in vascular endothelium and is first-line therapy for type 1 disease.
Plasma exchange treats TTP rather than an inherited vWF deficiency. Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency would make it appropriate.
Hydroxyurea prevents sickle-cell complications and does not release endothelial vWF. Recurrent vaso-occlusive crises would support it.
Caplacizumab inhibits vWF in severe TTP and would oppose the desired hemostatic effect. Severe platelet-vWF microthrombosis would make it appropriate.

question: A patient with the most severe inherited von Willebrand disorder has major bleeding. Prior desmopressin produced no response. Which treatment is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: Type 3 disease produces no vWF and therefore does not respond to desmopressin. Type 1 disease with concurrent iron loss would make this more appropriate.
Factor IX concentrate treats hemophilia B, not absent vWF. Documented Factor IX deficiency would make it correct.

options.text: Von Willebrand and Factor VIII concentrates
options.rationale: Type 3 von Willebrand disease requires vWF concentrate plus Factor VIII concentrate because endogenous vWF is absent.
Fresh frozen plasma is the listed therapy for hemophilia C. Factor XI deficiency would make it appropriate.
This treats immune-mediated TTP rather than inherited absence of vWF. Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency would make it appropriate.

question: A 32-year-old woman develops unilateral calf swelling after prolonged travel, followed by pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. D-dimer is 1,202 ng/mL [<500 ng/mL], and chest imaging shows a large pulmonary arterial clot. Which mechanism could create an inherited predisposition to this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: Reduced Factor VIII stabilization occurs with dysfunctional vWF and promotes bleeding rather than thrombosis. Procedure-related mucosal bleeding would support it.
Reduced ADAMTS13 causes platelet-vWF microthrombi, thrombocytopenia, and hemolysis rather than a typical inherited venous thrombophilia. Schistocytes would support it.
Absent vWF causes severe type 3 von Willebrand disease and bleeding. Major mucosal or hemophilia-like bleeding would make it appropriate.
Factor V Leiden causes Factor Va resistance to activated protein C, increasing thrombin production and venous thrombosis risk.
Reduced Factor XI causes hemophilia C and bleeding after trauma or procedures. Such bleeding rather than venous thrombosis would support it.

question: A patient with confirmed Factor V Leiden has now experienced a second separate venous thromboembolic event. Which long-term management is recommended?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: Plasma exchange treats TTP and does not address recurrent Factor V Leiden thrombosis. ADAMTS13-mediated microangiopathy would make it appropriate.
Vitamin B12 replacement treats deficiency-related macrocytosis and neuropathy. Low B12 with neurologic findings would make it appropriate.
Factor VIII prophylaxis treats hemophilia A and could increase hemostasis rather than prevent venous thrombosis. Factor VIII deficiency would support it.
Exchange transfusion treats hypoxic acute chest syndrome in sickle cell anemia. A new infiltrate with hypoxia would make it appropriate.
Lifetime anticoagulation is recommended for Factor V Leiden with more than one thromboembolic event.

question: A 32-year-old man has six weeks of painless cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, night sweats, low-grade fever, and splenomegaly. ESR is 95 mm/hr [0-22 mm/hr], and LDH is 486 U/L [100-190 U/L]. Which finding would establish the diagnosis?
cited_learning_objective: To review clinical vignettes illustrating frequently encountered disorders of red blood cells, of coagulation and of white blood cells.

options.rationale: The presentation suggests Hodgkin lymphoma, which is established by excisional node biopsy demonstrating Reed-Sternberg cells.
Schistocytes indicate microangiopathic hemolysis rather than Hodgkin lymphoma. Thrombocytopenia and kidney or neurologic injury would make them diagnostic clues.
Sickle cells support sickle cell anemia rather than a nodal malignancy. Pain crises or acute chest findings would make them relevant.
Absent ristocetin aggregation supports von Willebrand disease. Mucosal or procedure-related bleeding would make it appropriate.
Persistent thrombin after activated protein C supports Factor V Leiden. Recurrent venous thrombosis would make it appropriate.

question: A 45-year-old patient with Hodgkin lymphoma has night sweats, ESR of 92 mm/hr [0-22 mm/hr], and bulky nodal disease. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to understand the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of these blood disorders.

options.rationale: The listed findings are relapse-risk factors, not predictors of reduced bleeding. A hemostatic disorder would be required for a bleeding interpretation.
Age over 40 years, B symptoms, high ESR, and bulky adenopathy are all listed factors associated with Hodgkin lymphoma relapse.
Vitamin B12 deficiency requires macrocytosis, low B12, or supportive methylmalonic acid findings. Those changes would make this interpretation appropriate.
The features describe lymphoma prognosis rather than platelet dysfunction. Mucocutaneous bleeding and abnormal ristocetin aggregation would support platelet-vWF dysfunction.
Hodgkin lymphoma can spread hematogenously to marrow, liver, and lung. Evidence showing disease confined to contiguous nodes would be needed for this claim.

question: A patient presents with pallor, petechiae, and unexplained lymphadenopathy. Which initial test set most appropriately surveys red cells, white cells, platelets, morphology, and coagulation?
cited_learning_objective: To begin to develop an approach to a patient presenting with symptoms and signs of a blood disorder.

options.rationale: These tests refine an anemia evaluation but do not broadly assess leukocytes, platelets, morphology, and both coagulation pathways. Confirmed anemia would make them appropriate next tests.
These are considered when malignancy is suspected but do not provide the complete initial hematologic survey. A focused malignancy workup would make them appropriate.
The initial evaluation includes a CBC with differential, peripheral smear review, PT/INR, and aPTT.
These tests are used after anemia is identified and do not fully assess leukocytes, platelets, or coagulation. Established anemia would make them appropriate.
This combines diagnostic and treatment steps for established malignancy rather than initial evaluation. Confirmed Hodgkin lymphoma would make these steps relevant.
